title: Why Important Questions Are Often Difficult: Significance, Persistence, and the Composition of Unresolved Inquiry
author: Honggao Cao
abstract: Why do questions that matter so much often remain difficult to answer? This paper distinguishes obstacles to resolving a particular question from the processes that shape which questions remain under active inquiry. Questions may stay open because evidence, methods, or other necessary conditions are missing. Across a population, difficulty can slow resolution while significance can sustain pursuit. As more tractable questions are answered and less-valued inquiries are dropped, the remaining active questions can become richer in both significance and difficulty. A competing-risks model shows that this enrichment does not necessarily create statistical dependence: with independent attributes at entry and separable survival weights, the two properties remain independent among survivors. Examples from disease research, mathematics, markets, and artificial intelligence distinguish persistent obstacles from changing questions. The practical task is to identify why a particular inquiry remains open before deciding what further progress requires.

title: An Analytical Framework for Error and Hallucination in Deployed Generative AI Systems
author: Honggao Cao
abstract: Judging a response from a deployed generative AI system requires an applicable standard; explaining its production requires a different evidentiary basis. These requirements can diverge: information used in production may differ from the information that should govern evaluation, and a valid error classification may leave the production cause unresolved. We develop an authority-first framework that addresses these problems in sequence. The evaluator establishes the task and applicable authority policy, identifies assessable assertions and task obligations, and selects the governing standards. Assertions are classified as supported, contradicted, unsupported, or unresolved; obligations are assessed as satisfied, violated, or unresolved. These parallel comparisons support two related error classifications. Hallucination concerns a representational assertion contradicted by, or lacking support required from, its governing reference. Task-obligation fidelity error concerns failure to satisfy an applicable requirement. The classifications can overlap when a response both violates a requirement and misrepresents compliance or the requirement itself. We then distinguish identifying an error from locating its possible production source and attributing its cause. Applications to temporal change, continuing-project state, propagation, and retrieval-augmented generation show how the distinction guides evaluation of configured systems. Consequences inform the urgency of a response, while supported production findings inform the choice of controls. The framework supplies a conceptual sequence whose effects on evaluator agreement and control selection remain questions for empirical study.
